chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qasani, both together from al-Qasim ibn Yahya, from Sulayman ibn Dawud, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

A man said to him, 'What is your view — if I see something in a man's hands, is it permissible for me to testify that it belongs to him?' He said: 'Yes.' The man said, 'I can testify that it is in his hand, but I cannot testify that it belongs to him, for perhaps it belongs to someone else.'

So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Is it then permissible to buy it from him?' He said, 'Yes.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'But perhaps it belongs to someone else — so from where is it permissible for you to buy it and have ownership transfer to you, then after acquiring ownership say «it is mine» and swear an oath over it, yet not be permitted to attribute it to the one from whom its ownership came to you?'
Then Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'If this were not permissible, no market would be established for the Muslims.'

key_terms.شهادة: Testimony — formal legal witness statement in Islamic law
key_terms.ملك: Ownership/property — legal possession with full rights
key_terms.يد: Hand/possession — in Islamic jurisprudence, 'yad' (possession/hand) is a recognized basis for establishing presumptive ownership

ai.seo_question: Is possession sufficient evidence for testifying about ownership in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes the legal principle that physical possession (yad) serves as sufficient presumptive evidence for ownership, enabling both testimony and commercial transactions. Through a Socratic dialogue, the Imam exposes the inconsistency of accepting possession-based transactions while rejecting possession-based testimony. The ruling reflects the foundational Islamic commercial principle that without such a presumption of ownership, commerce and market exchange would be impossible.
